Patient Vignette: QA Engineer, Age 24

He still thinks about the smoke. Not the thick, black kind you see in movies, but a thin, gray haze that smelled of burnt plastic and something else-something sweet and wrong. He was in the server room when the fire alarm went off. It was a Tuesday, 3:47 PM, and he was running a regression test on the new deployment. He remembers the exact time because he had just logged the test results in his ticket.

The fire started in the electrical closet two floors below. By the time he and his team evacuated, the building was already filling with that strange, chemical smoke. He walked down twelve flights of stairs, his hand on the railing, his heart hammering in his throat. He didn't panic. He was calm. He helped a junior developer who was shaking and told her it was just a drill. It wasn't.

He has not been back to that office. The company relocated to a temporary space three weeks later, but he cannot make himself walk through the glass doors. He works from home now, his manager has approved it, but every morning he feels a knot in his stomach as he opens his laptop. He is a QA engineer. His job is to find bugs, to anticipate failure, to make sure everything runs smoothly. He used to love that. Now, every time his terminal logs an error, he feels a jolt of adrenaline, like the world is about to catch fire again.

He avoids crowds. He used to go to concerts, to the crowded taquería on Saturday nights, to his cousin's birthday parties. Now, he tells people he is busy. He tells them he has a deadline. The truth is, he cannot stand the feeling of being surrounded, of not being able to see the exit. He scans every room he enters, looking for doors, for windows, for anything that might let him out. He does this without thinking. It is automatic now, like breathing.

Sleep is difficult. He falls asleep easily, but he wakes up at 3:47 AM most nights, his heart racing, his palms damp. He does not remember the dream, only the feeling of terror, the smell of that sweet, wrong smoke. He lies in the dark, listening to the hum of his air conditioner, reminding himself that he is safe, that the building is not on fire, that he is in his apartment. It takes him an hour to fall back asleep.

He stopped dating six months ago. He went on two dates after the fire, and both times he felt a creeping unease, a sense that he needed to leave, that something bad was about to happen. He excused himself to the bathroom and almost walked out of the restaurant. He hasn't tried since. He tells himself he is focusing on his career.

His mother calls him every Sunday. She asks how he is, and he says he is fine. He says work is good. He does not tell her about the nightmares, about the way his hands shake when he hears a siren, about the fact that he has not been inside a building taller than two stories since the fire. He does not tell her that he sometimes takes the long way home to avoid passing the old office.

He has a PCL-5 score of 56. He does not know this. He only knows that he is tired, that he is jumpy, that he cannot seem to shake the feeling that something is about to go wrong. He is good at his job. He finds the bugs. But he cannot find the one inside himself. He does not know how to test for that.
